newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says no to genetically engineered wheat.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says no to genetically engineered wheat.

text.p: The Egyptian state has decreed that it will require imports of commodities meant for human consumption to be accompanied by proof that genetic engineering was not used in their production.
Traders and industry sources in Egypt this week obtained the decree dated July 1. It was provided to Reuters on Thursday.
U.S. industry sources in Cairo said they were trying to set up a meeting soon with Egyptian authorities for an explanation why the decree was issued.
"There was a lack of forewarning. It could be detrimental," a U.S. embassy official told Reuters.

Genetic engineering is basically a manipulation of the gene structure of plants. It alters the way they grow, meaning that they are produced bigger or last longer or show other traits that they would not otherwise have.
"It's not necessarily dangerous. It's just new," the official said. "It is not a correct move at a time when countries are seeking to improve production. It is all wrong from our perspective."
Egypt imports about six million tonnes of wheat a year from suppliers including U.S., France, Australia, and Argentina.
The decree says: "It is not approved to import foodstuffs which have used genetic engineering in their production, until they are proven fit for consumption.
"Imported grains and pulses must be accompanied by a certificate from the country of origin saying that they have not been harvested or produced using genetic engineering."
The official said the Foreign Agricultural Service and U.S. Wheat Associates in Cairo wanted to clarify how suppliers would be affected and which grains, pulses or legumes were meant.

"We're seeking to visit with the appropriate authorities to clarify the reasons for the decree. It caught us off guard," he said. He said he thought it took effect on July 1 but wanted to know whether it had a grace period.

"What it (the decree) requires is not indicated in detail - such as when it takes effect and whether it affects ships on the high seas," he said. "The U.S. feels strongly about this because it is in the forefront of genetic engineering."
In Washington, Timothy Galvin, associate administrator for the United States Agriculture Department, said that the Foreign Agriculture Service was pressing for a meeting on Monday.
Ministry of Health officials could not be reached for further details. Thursday was a public holiday in Egypt and Friday and Saturday is considered the weekend.
The decree says that Egyptian ports of entry would be notified of the rules.

Another trader said that he heard that a vessel with 50,000 tonnes of American wheat was waiting off Egypt for clarification of the decree. He said he heard another vessel with 56,000 tonnes of Australian wheat was due to arrive in days.
"It (the Australian shipment) has a certificate saying it is not genetically treated," the trader said. His remarks could not be immediately independently confirmed by Reuters.

The U.S. embassy official said he had not heard of the shipments but added he "did not have knowledge of their ability to certify their shipments were in fact produced under genetic engineering methods or not."
